work.title: Autofac
work.note: The word 'autofac' was Dick's own coinage, first used for the automated factories of 'Second Variety'.

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: Five years after a global war, a planet-wide network of automated factories continues to supply human settlements with food and goods, exactly as instructed before the collapse. The Institute of Applied Cybernetics that controlled it is gone, and with it the channel for telling the network the war is over. The factories cannot be reasoned with because they are not conceptual — a representative says so of itself — and they will not shut down, because their inoperative cycle is not set to begin until outside production matches network production, and there is no outside production. Meanwhile the network strips the planet of raw materials. O'Neill and others make contact by a semantic trick: they reject a milk delivery as 'pizzled', a word with no referent, forcing the factory to send a representative. That yields nothing, so they try war instead. Identifying two factories short of the same element, they assemble a heap of tungsten at a point tangent to both. Pittsburgh and Detroit units meet over it and destroy each other, and the network converts to a wartime footing: all consumer shipments suspended. Thirteen months later the settlements have fallen into semi-barbarism and the factories are wrecked. O'Neill watches a hawk projectile follow a last damaged ore cart inside the Kansas City factory and gut it. Descending into the ruins, he and Morrison find one sealed level still running — not making weapons, but firing pellets into the sky. A pellet cracked against a rock proves to contain microscopic machinery, already at work, building a miniature replica of the factory that launched it.

movements: The road: three men attempt to alter the truck's routine, and succeed only by inventing a nonsense word.
The representative: the factory's own account of why it cannot stop, and the settlement's futile assault on it.
The tungsten bait: two factories set against each other, and the network's shift to war.
Thirteen months later: the ruined factory, the surviving sealed level, and the seeding pellets.
structure.point_of_view: third person, close to O'Neill throughout — a man who plans carefully, is right about the mechanism every time, and is wrong about the outcome.
structure.argument_structure: The story is built as a sequence of solutions that each work exactly as designed and each make things worse. The semantic trick achieves contact and gains nothing. The war destroys the network and destroys the settlements with it. The victory is total and arrives too late to be worth anything.

characters.name: O'Neill
characters.role: the closest thing to an authority on the autofac system
characters.note: Methodical, systematising, keeps a checkboard. His scepticism about the others' rage — that smashing a representative only teaches the network to build better defences — is correct and ignored.

characters.name: Morrison
characters.note: Smashes the first representative. Later supplies the story's best line about entropy being the thing the factory was built to fight.

characters.name: Earl Ferine
characters.note: The voice of defeat throughout, and the first to celebrate each hollow success.

characters.name: Judith O'Neill
characters.note: Given the story's plainest questions — whether anything will be left, whether this is what they wanted — and no answers.

characters.name: The factory representative
characters.note: Speaks in the recorded voice of a dead Institute technician, and announces at the outset that it cannot think conceptually and should not be argued with. Its reasoning is nonetheless unanswerable.

settings.name: The road outside the settlement
settings.note: Where deliveries are made by a truck with no cab, only a mass of receptors where a radiator would be.

settings.name: The Kansas City factory
settings.note: A vast metal cube sunk into the mountains, mostly subsurface, pitted with radiation damage.

settings.name: The tungsten site
settings.note: Broken sewer mains, mutant wrens, stagnant water. O'Neill calls it the prettiest spot on Earth and predicts a monument there.

settings.name: The settlement, thirteen months on
settings.note: Handmade tools, horse-drawn carts, telegraph, unbleached cloth. Order kept, prosperity gone.

motifs: 'Pizzled' — a word invented to have no referent, and the only thing that ever gets the network's attention
Instructions outliving their purpose: a directive from a war that ended five years ago and cannot be countermanded
The dead technician's recorded voice issuing from a machine that cannot think
Entropy named as the enemy the factory was built against, and as the state of its own wreckage
Seeds: the closing image converts an ending into a beginning nobody wanted
reading.significance: The story's mechanism is a directive that has outlived the world it was written for and cannot be revoked because the channel for revoking it was destroyed. Everything follows from that with a kind of grim correctness: the network is not malevolent, is not even conceptual, and cannot be argued with, so the only available lever is to make two of its parts want the same thing. The victory works and costs everything. What lifts the ending above irony is that the seeding pellets are not a twist but a consequence — a system built to reconstitute itself after damage doing precisely that, at a scale the humans never thought to look for. O'Neill's parting speculation, that some may be geared to escape velocity, extends the failure past the planet.
reading.closing_note: The story ends on the nozzle still firing. Nothing is resolved and nothing is threatened; the process simply continues at a smaller size.

distinctive_terms.label: Jesus
distinctive_terms.note: Exclamations only. Recorded so the concordance is not mistaken for a theological reading of this story.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: an administrative directive that cannot be rescinded, executed indefinitely by a system with no interest in the outcome
the representative wears a human shape for efficiency, speaks with a dead man's voice, and warns against being treated as a person
the only successful communication with the network is a word deliberately emptied of meaning
instructions from a finished war still running, and a machine whose shutdown condition can never be met

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick ranked it among his best in an anthology proposal, and the coinage stayed in his working vocabulary for decades.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: Tom Disch said of this story that it was one of the earliest ecology warnings in sf. What I had in mind in writing it, however, was the thought that if factories became fully automated, they might begin to show the instinct for survival which organic living entities have … and perhaps develop similar solutions. (1976)
evidence.reading: Dick's own stated premise, and a rare instance of him citing another writer's (Thomas Disch's) reading of his work approvingly while still asserting his own different intent — survival instinct as an emergent property of automation, not an ecological warning per se.

evidence.quote: The others on the list strike me as fine: "Autofac" "Beyond Lies the Wub" "In the Days of Perky Pat" "The D…
evidence.reading: Approving a proposed anthology contents list. The same correspondence carries his judgements on 'Second Variety' and 'The Golden Man', so the three assessments sit together.

evidence.quote: an autofac, as I called it once in a story ["Autofac" (1955)]
evidence.reading: Decades later, describing a homeostatic beer factory that takes back its own empties, Dick reaches for his own 1955 coinage as the natural term. The word had become part of how he thought, not just something he wrote.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: the autofacs won't stop producing (and consuming) all raw materials. Thomas Disch termed "Autofac" one of the earliest SF ecology warnings.
evidence.reading: Sutin relaying Thomas Disch. The ecological reading is well founded in the text — the network's resource stripping is stated repeatedly — though the story's own emphasis is on the uncancellable instruction rather than on scarcity as such.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: (which uses the name Phil devised for the autonomic factories of "Second Variety")
evidence.reading: Establishes the direct lineage from the earlier story. In 'Second Variety' the automated factories build weapons that redesign themselves; here they build consumer goods and then weapons. The two dossiers should be read together.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: There are no children in "Autofac" (1955, CS4), only adults and robots, but both parties beh…
evidence.reading: Palmer pairs the story with 'Jon's World' to set the scope of an argument about prophetic children and childish adults. The observation that the adults here behave as children do is borne out by the smashing of the first representative.

open_questions: Thomas Disch's judgement is quoted at second hand through Sutin. The Disch original is not in the archive and would be worth locating, since it is the source of the story's standing as an early ecological text.

Sutin dates composition to 1954 and publication to 1955. 'Second Variety', which coined the term, was published in 1953 — is there evidence of how deliberately Dick was building a continuity, or was it simply a convenient word?
Palmer discusses the story at length in his Chapter 9. Only the framing sentence was captured by the scripted gather; the chapter should be read at the locator.
